\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 32\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Surgical Management of Upper GI Bleeding\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Surgery is now less common because modern endoscopic and radiological techniques are\u003cbr>highly effective. However, surgery remains essential in:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 33\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. uncontrolled hemorrhage,\u003cbr>2. recurrent bleeding,\u003cbr>3. perforated ulcers,\u003cbr>4. failed embolization,\u003cbr>5. or hemodynamic collapse.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to surgical gastroenterology principles, surgery is considered when: bleeding\u003cbr>cannot be controlled endoscopically, more than 4–6 units of blood are rapidly required or\u003cbr>recurrent life-threatening hemorrhage occurs.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">BUT surgery is less commonly used today because: TIPS has largely replaced surgical  shunts\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">However, surgical shunts such as: splenorenal shunt, portocaval shunt may occasionally be\u003cbr>considered where expertise exists. These procedures reduce portal pressure by diverting\u003cbr>portal blood into systemic circulation.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Complications of Surgery\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Surgical intervention carries significant risks, especially in: elderly patients, cirrhotics,\u003cbr>shocked patients, and patients with multiorgan failure.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Complications include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. infection,\u003cbr>2. anastomotic leak,\u003cbr>3. Renal failure,\u003cbr>4. respiratory failure,\u003cbr>5. rebleeding,\u003cbr>6. and postoperative mortality.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Therefore, surgery is usually reserved for: Rescue therapy after failure of less invasive\u003cbr>methods. ICU and Multidisciplinary Care;\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>POST-ENDOSCOPIC MANAGEMENT IN UPPER\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>GASTROINTESTINAL BLEEDING\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">After successful endoscopic Haemostasis, management does not end. The: Post-endoscopic\u003cbr>phase is extremely important because many patients may develop:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. early rebleeding,\u003cbr>2. infection,\u003cbr>3. shock recurrence,\u003cbr>4. Renal failure,\u003cbr>5. hepatic decompensation,\u003cbr>6. or delayed complications.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, Harrison’s Internal Medicine,\u003cbr>ACG guidelines, and hepatology recommendations, post-endoscopic care focuses on:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 34\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">prevention of rebleeding,  treatment of the underlying disease, optimization of organ\u003cbr>function, monitoring for complications, and long-term prevention strategies.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The management differs significantly between:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  variceal bleeding,   •  and non-variceal bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Immediate Monitoring After Endoscopy\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">After endoscopic intervention, patients require close monitoring because the first:24–72\u003cbr>hours carry the highest risk of recurrent hemorrhage.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Monitoring should include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. blood pressure,\u003cbr>2. pulse rate,\u003cbr>3. respiratory rate,\u003cbr>4. oxygen saturation,\u003cbr>5. mental status,\u003cbr>6. urine output,\u003cbr>7. stool color,\u003cbr>8. recurrence of hematemesis,\u003cbr>9. and serial hemoglobin measurements.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Signs suggesting:Rebleeding\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. fresh hematemesis,\u003cbr>2. worsening melena,\u003cbr>3. hypotension,\u003cbr>4. Tachycardia,\u003cbr>5. falling hemoglobin,\u003cbr>6. rising lactate,\u003cbr>7. and recurrent shock.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients with severe cirrhosis, major transfusion requirements, or persistent instability may\u003cbr>require ICU-level monitoring.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Continued Pharmacological Therapy\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">After Variceal Bleeding Patients with Variceal bleeding continue:  Vasoactive therapy\u003cbr>even after successful endoscopy. Commonly: Octreotide infusion continues for\u003cbr>approximately 2–5 days.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The reason is continued reduction of: portal venous inflow, portal pressure and variceal wall  tension.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 35\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This significantly reduces: Early rebleeding risk which is highest during the first few days\u003cbr>after hemorrhage. According to portal hypertension guidelines, stopping vasoactive therapy\u003cbr>too early may increase recurrent bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Antibiotics in Cirrhotic Patients - All cirrhotic patients with UGIB should\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">continue: Antibiotic prophylaxis usually for: 5–7 days\u003cbr>2. Proton Pump Inhibitors After Non-Variceal Bleeding- Peptic ulcer bleeding\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">PPIs are continued after endoscopic therapy. High-risk ulcers often require: IV\u003cbr>PPI initially, followed by oral PPI therapy. The purpose of continued acid\u003cbr>suppression is:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. clot stabilization,\u003cbr>2. ulcer healing,\u003cbr>3. prevention of recurrent hemorrhage,\u003cbr>4. and reduction of acid-mediated fibrinolysis.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Common regimens include: Pantoprazole, Omeprazole and Esomeprazole.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">According to ACG and ESGE guidelines, high-risk ulcers benefit significantly from\u003cbr>continued PPI therapy after endoscopic haemostasis.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Management of Portal Hypertension\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In patients with cirrhosis and variceal bleeding, long-term management of:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Portal hypertension is Essential. On-Selective Beta Blockers\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patients are usually started on: Propranolol, Nadolol, or Carvedilol.\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 35\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 35\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 36\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">These drugs reduce portal pressure through: β1 blockade → reduced cardiac output, β2\u003cbr>blockade → splanchnic vasoconstriction. This reduces portal venous inflow, variceal wall\u003cbr>tension and recurrent hemorrhage risk. According to Baveno and hepatology guidelines:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Combination therapy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">using: beta blockers, plus, repeated EVL provides the best secondary prevention against\u003cbr>recurrent variceal bleeding. Repeat Endoscopic Variceal Ligation (EVL) Varices are rarely\u003cbr>cured after one session. Therefore: Repeat EVL is usually performed every: 2–4 weeks until:\u003cbr>Variceal obliteration is achieved. This reduces recurrent hemorrhage and mortality\u003cbr>significantly.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Management of Ascites and Fluid Retention\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Many cirrhotic patients develop ascites, peripheral edema, and fluid overload.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Management includes:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. sodium restriction,   2. spironolactone,   3. and furosemide.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The commonly recommended ratio is: Spironolactone: Furosemide = 100: 40 or\u003cbr>approximately:1 : 4 This ratio helps maintain potassium balance. Spironolactone is\u003cbr>particularly effective because hyperaldosteronism is a major mechanism of sodium retention\u003cbr>in cirrhosis.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Prevention and Management of Hepatic Encephalopathy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">After variceal hemorrhage, patients are at increased risk of: Hepatic encephalopathy\u003cbr>because: blood proteins increase ammonia production, portal-systemic shunting increases,\u003cbr>and infection may precipitate encephalopathy.  Management includes: Lactulose, correction\u003cbr>of precipitating factors, treatment of infection, electrolyte correction, and nutritional\u003cbr>optimization.  Lactulose reduces ammonia absorption by: acidifying the colon, trapping\u003cbr>ammonia as ammonium, and increasing bowel transit.\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 36\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 36\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 37\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Management of H. pylori in Peptic Ulcer Disease\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In non-variceal bleeding caused by peptic ulcer disease: H. pylori eradication is essential.\u003cbr>Persistent H. pylori infection strongly increases recurrent ulcer formation, recurrent bleeding,\u003cbr>and ulcer complications.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Common triple therapy includes PPI, Clarithromycin, Amoxicillin depending on local\u003cbr>resistance patterns. According to gastroenterology guidelines, eradication therapy\u003cbr>dramatically reduces recurrent ulcer bleeding.\u003c/p>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 37\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,
